title: Word Problem Detective
goal: I can ask 3 detective questions and pick add, subtract or multiply.

card.desc: Bristol learns a 3-question detective routine for every word problem: What is happening? Are there equal groups? Which operation? She sorts add, subtract and multiply stories and matches each story to a picture. This goes after her biggest math habit: grabbing the numbers and picking the wrong operation.

win: Case closed! You are a real word problem detective!

slides.title: Detective Practice
slides.text: You learned the 3 detective questions with Jonathan. Now be a detective on your own! 🔍

slides.title: The 3 detective questions

steps.text: 1. What is happening?
2. Are there equal groups? Look for each, every, per.
3. Which operation? ➕ join different amounts · ➖ take away or compare · ✖️ equal groups

slides.tip: How many more means compare. Compare means subtract.

slides.title: Say it out loud
slides.text: Say these out loud. You can tell your mom!
prompts: Say the 3 detective questions without looking.
Tell an equal groups story about puppies.
Tell a take away story about treats.

items.q:
There are 4 kennels. Each kennel has 5 puppies. How many puppies?
Which operation?
items.no: Look for the word each. Is every kennel the same?

items.q:
Ellie picked 9 apples. Liz picked 6 apples. How many apples did they pick?
Which operation?
items.why: 9 and 6 are different amounts. They join → add. 9 + 6 = 15.
items.no: Are 9 and 6 equal groups? Do they join or go away?

items.q:
Marion had 16 balloons. 7 popped. How many are left?
Which operation?
items.no: Did balloons join, or did some go away?

slides.title: Add, subtract or multiply?
slides.text: Tap a story. Then tap the right box.

items.text: There are 3 bikes. Each bike has 2 wheels.
Amy found 8 shells. Then she found 6 more.
items.hint: Did shells join or go away?

items.text: Liz has 20 grapes. Ellie has 12. How many more does Liz have?
Every one of the 5 kittens drinks 2 bowls of milk.
There were 14 kids at the park. 5 went home.
Marion has 4 red pens and 9 blue pens.
items.why: 4 and 9 are different amounts. They join. Add.

slides.done: Great detective work! Equal groups ✖️, join ➕, take away or compare ➖.

slides.title: Find the answer
slides.text: Ask the 3 questions. Then type the answer.

items.q: There are 4 cages. Each cage has 7 birds. How many birds?
items.why: Equal groups: 4 × 7. Double 7 is 14. Double 14 is 28.
items.no: Each cage has 7. Make 4 groups of 7. Then check your math.

items.q: Ellie had 25 beads. She used 9 on a bracelet. How many are left?
items.why: She used some, so subtract. 25 − 9 = 16. Check: 16 + 9 = 25.
items.no: She used beads. They went away. Then check your math.

items.q: Liz has 13 stickers. Amy has 8. How many more does Liz have?
items.no: How many more means compare. Subtract. Then check your math.

items.q: There are 2 bowls. Each bowl has 9 fish snacks. What would you draw?
choices: A bowl of 2 snacks and a bowl of 9 snacks
no: That switches them. How many bowls?
Each bowl has 9. The bowls are equal.

items.q: Amy had 11 marbles. She gave 4 to Liz. What would you draw?
items.why: She gave away 4, so cross them out. 11 − 4 = 7.
no: Amy did not get more. She gave 4 away.
There are no equal groups here.

items.q: There are 7 packs. Each pack has 3 bows. How many bows in all?
items.why: In all does not always mean add. Each pack has 3. 7 × 3 = 21.
items.no: Each pack has 3. Is it equal groups? Then check your math.

items.q: Marion has 17 crayons. Liz has 9. How many more does Marion have?
items.no: Compare the two girls. Subtract. Then check your math.

items.q: Which words tell you to compare?
items.why: How many more asks you to compare. Then you subtract.
no: In all can mean add or multiply. It does not compare.
Each tells you the groups are equal.

items.why: 8 × 9 = 72. Check: 10 eights is 80. Take away one 8: 72. ✔
items.no: What times 8 makes 72? Use the 9s trick.
items.hint: 10 eights is 80. Take away one 8: 72. How many eights is that?

sets.q: Ellie has 6 bags. There are 8 marbles in each bag. How many marbles in all?
sets.no: Each bag has 8. Is it equal groups? Then check your math.

sets.q: Liz had 17 stickers. She gave 9 to Amy. How many does Liz have now?
sets.why: She gave some away, so subtract. 17 − 9 = 8.
sets.no: Did stickers join or go away? Then check your math.

sets.q: Which story needs subtract?
choices: There are 4 cats. Each cat has 2 bowls.
Amy has 12 pens. Marion has 7. How many more does Amy have?
Liz walked 6 dogs. Then she walked 5 more dogs.
no: Each cat has 2. That is multiply.
She walked 5 more. They join. That is add.

sets.q: 7 kids each bring 4 cans of dog food. Which number sentence fits?
sets.why: Each kid brings 4. 7 equal groups of 4: 7 × 4 = 28.
no: Each kid brings 4. That is equal groups.
No cans go away.

sets.q: Which story matches this picture?
choices: 3 pens with 5 puppies in each pen
5 pens with 3 puppies in each pen
sets.why: The picture has 3 groups. Each group has 5.
no: Count the groups in the picture. There are 3.
The picture shows equal groups.

sets.q: Marion, Ellie, Liz and Amy each have 9 ribbons. How many ribbons?
sets.no: Count the girls. Each one has 9.

sets.q: Amy read 28 pages on Monday. She read 16 pages on Tuesday. How many pages did she read?
sets.no: 28 and 16 are different. Do they join? Then check your math.

sets.q:
Ellie says: 8 vases. Each vase has 7 flowers. So 8 + 7 = 15 flowers.
How many flowers are there really?
sets.why: Each vase has 7. Equal groups, so multiply. 8 × 7 = 56.
sets.no: Ellie added. Each vase has 7, so multiply. Then check your math.

sets.q: There are 7 tanks. Each tank has 6 fish. How many fish?
sets.no: Each tank has 6. Is it equal groups? Then check your math.

sets.q: Marion had 23 crayons. She lost 8. How many are left?
sets.no: Did crayons join or go away? Then check your math.

sets.q: Which story should you solve with add?
choices: There are 5 boxes with 4 cups in each.
Ellie had 14 cards. She gave away 6.
Liz has 9 red beads and 7 blue beads.
sets.why: 9 red and 7 blue are different amounts that join. 9 + 7 = 16.
no: 4 cups in each box. That is multiply.
She gave cards away. That is subtract.

sets.q: There are 9 bikes. Every bike has 2 wheels. Which number sentence fits?
no: Every bike has 2 wheels. That is equal groups.
No wheels go away.

sets.q: Look at the picture. Which story fits it?
sets.why: The picture has 4 groups. Each group has 6.
no: Count the groups in the picture. There are 4.
The picture shows equal groups.

sets.q: Each of the 4 Critter Club girls brings 8 dog treats. How many treats?
sets.no: Each girl brings 8. Is it equal groups? Then check your math.

sets.q: Liz counted 37 birds in the morning and 26 birds after lunch. How many birds did she count?
sets.no: 37 and 26 are different. Do they join? Then check your math.

sets.q:
Marion says: 9 cages. Each cage has 4 mice. So 9 + 4 = 13 mice.
How many mice are there really?
sets.why: Each cage has 4. Equal groups, so multiply. 9 × 4 = 36.
sets.no: Marion added. Each cage has 4, so multiply. Then check your math.

sets.q: There are 8 vans. Each van has 7 kids. How many kids?
sets.no: Each van has 7. Is it equal groups? Then check your math.

sets.q: The vet had 31 bandages. She used 14. How many are left?
sets.no: Did bandages join or go away? Then check your math.

sets.q: Which story should you solve with multiply?
choices: There are 6 hutches. Each hutch has 3 rabbits.
no: Hats and scarves are different amounts. That is add.
She lost bows. That is subtract.

sets.q: There are 5 plates. Every plate has 9 grapes. Which number sentence fits?
no: Every plate has 9. That is equal groups.
There are 5 plates, not 9.

sets.q: Which story does this picture show?
sets.why: The picture has 5 groups. Each group has 4.
no: Count the groups in the picture. There are 5.
The picture shows equal groups.

sets.q: Amy fills 9 bowls. She puts 6 scoops in every bowl. How many scoops?
sets.no: Every bowl has 6. Is it equal groups? Then check your math.

sets.q: Ellie read 45 pages last week and 38 pages this week. How many pages did she read?
sets.no: 45 and 38 are different. Do they join? Then check your math.

sets.q:
Liz says: 7 rows. Each row has 9 carrots. So 7 + 9 = 16 carrots.
How many carrots are there really?
sets.why: Each row has 9. Equal groups, so multiply. 7 × 9 = 63.
sets.no: Liz added. Each row has 9, so multiply. Then check your math.

practice.intro: Three tries on each one. Only your first try counts. Ask the 3 detective questions first!

questions.q:
There were 12 birds. 5 flew away.
Add, subtract or multiply?
questions.why: 5 birds went away. Take away → subtract. 12 − 5 = 7.

questions.q:
There are 5 tanks. Each tank has 3 turtles.
Add, subtract or multiply?
Liz has 7 hair clips. Amy has 9 hair clips. How many hair clips in all?
questions.no: The girls have different amounts. Do they join? Then check your math.

questions.q: There are 8 tables. Every table has 4 cups. How many cups?
questions.why: 8 equal groups of 4. Double 8 is 16. Double 16 is 32.
questions.no: Every table has 4. Multiply. Then check your math.

questions.q: Marion has 15 ribbons. Ellie has 6. How many more does Marion have?
questions.no: How many more means subtract. Then check your math.

questions.q: Amy has 3 fish tanks. Each tank has 9 fish. What would you draw?
choices: A group of 3 fish and a group of 9 fish
no: That switches them. How many tanks?
Each tank has 9. That is equal groups.

questions.q: 6 dogs each wear 4 boots. How many boots?
questions.no: Every dog wears 4 boots. Multiply. Then check your math.

choices: There are 7 vans with 6 kids in each van.
Amy saw 8 cats and 5 dogs at the vet.
no: Each van has 6. That is multiply.
She used 4. That is subtract.

questions.q: A box had 16 dog treats. The puppy ate 9. How many are left?
questions.no: The puppy ate some. Subtract. Then check your math.
questions.hint: Check your answer: it + 9 should make 16.

questions.q: There are 7 rows of carrots in the garden. Each row has 7 carrots. How many carrots?
no: 14 is 7 + 7. That is only 2 rows.
42 is 6 × 7. There are 7 rows.

questions.q:
Ellie buys 5 packs. There are 8 cards in every pack.
Which words tell you it is equal groups?
questions.why: In every pack means each pack has the same number: 8.
no: Those words do not tell how many are in each pack.
5 packs tells how many groups. Which words say each pack is the same?

questions.q: Marion has 6 jars. Each jar has 9 buttons. How many buttons?
questions.no: Each jar has 9. Multiply. Then check your math.

pages.title: Part 1: Detective questions
pages.directions: Read the story. Circle Add, Subtract or Multiply. Then solve.

items.text: 1. The shelter has 9 kennels. Each kennel has 4 puppies. How many puppies?
2. Liz had 13 beads. She lost 5 beads. How many beads are left?
3. Ellie has 9 stamps. Marion has 7 stamps. How many stamps in all?
4. Marion has 15 shells. Liz has 8 shells. How many more does Marion have?

pages.title: Part 2: Draw it
pages.directions: Draw a picture. Then write the number sentence.

items.text: 5. There are 3 bowls. Each bowl has 8 berries. How many berries?
6. Amy has 12 grapes. She eats 4. How many are left? Draw 12 grapes. Cross out the ones she eats.

pages.title: Part 3: Be the teacher
pages.directions: Is Liz right? Write the right number sentence.

items.text: 7. Liz says: 7 dogs. Each dog has 2 ears. 7 + 2 = 9 ears.

pages.title: Part 4: Book corner
pages.directions: Use a capital letter and a period.

items.text: 8. Write one clue from your book.

teacher.objective: Bristol uses a 3-question routine (What is happening? Equal groups or not? Which operation?) to choose add, subtract or multiply in one-step word problems, and matches each story to a picture. This is Week 4 Day 1 (Learn it) toward mastering Pathways Week 7 Math.
materials: Zoom with screen share (open the Class lesson from the course page, code 9110)
Zoom whiteboard (or paper and marker to hold up to the camera) for you to draw her stories
At her home: about 20 beans, coins or blocks, a sheet of paper and a pencil
Her book, Amy and the Missing Puppy
Packet (2 pages) for Tia to print this week (it is due Thursday, on Tuesday's task list)

plan.do: Class slide 1. Share your screen. Check she has beans, paper, pencil and her book.
Class slide 2. Where she stopped, a real clue from the text, what she would do as Amy.
Class slide 3. She names the strategy before each answer (double the 4s; 10 groups take away one; equal shelves → multiply).
Class slide 4. She builds 4 piles of 6 beans and proves 4 + 6 = 10 is wrong.
Class slides 5–6. She says the 3 questions from memory, then acts out join, take away and equal groups with beans on camera.
Class slide 7. Beans first (5 piles of 3), then she tells you the numbers for the screen.
Class slide 8. She reads each card aloud and says what is happening BEFORE choosing a box.
Class slides 9–10. You model 7 dogs × 4 treats on the whiteboard; then she leads the 6 + 9 cats story, answering each question before you reveal it.
Class slide 11. She describes her picture before looking at the choices.
Class slides 12–13. "In all" can be multiply; "how many more" is subtract.

plan.block: Detective steps + tell me a story
plan.do: Class slides 14–15. She orders the steps, then makes up stories for 6 × 4, 6 + 4 and 10 − 4 while you draw them.
Class slide 16. She answers the 3 questions out loud on each story before giving the answer.
Class slide 17. She says the 3 questions from memory. Show tonight's task list: the After-Class Lesson (it ends with Show What You Know) and 10 minutes of reading. Nothing else tonight.

watch: Grabbing the two numbers and adding (14 + 8 for "how many more"). Ask: "What is happening? Is something joining or are we comparing?"
Thinking "in all" always means add. Point to each/every and ask: are the groups equal?
Subtracting in the wrong order (8 − 14). Ask: which amount is bigger? Start with the bigger one.
Swapping groups and each (6 hutches of 3 for 3 hutches of 6). Ask: what are the groups? How many are in each?
Facts 6–9 from Weeks 2–3 (54 for 8 × 7, or 45 for 9 × 6). Name the strategy: double the 4s, or 10 groups take away one.

packet_key.answer: 3 bowls with 8 berries in each; 3 × 8 = 24 berries
No. Each dog has 2 ears, so multiply: 7 × 2 = 14 ears
Any clue from the book in a complete sentence with a capital letter and a period.

teacher.notes: Tonight is light on purpose: only the After-Class Lesson (which ends with Show What You Know, 3 question sets that rotate on retakes) and 10 minutes of reading. This lesson's Practice and Packet are on Tuesday's task list, due Thursday. Check her score before Tuesday's class. If she scores under 85, open Lesson 10 with 10 minutes of acting out stories with real objects (join, take away, compare, equal groups) and have her retake Show What You Know (she gets a new set) before she starts the Lesson 10 After-Class Lesson. Keep asking the 3 questions in every math lesson from now on.

tasks: Monday night: do the After-Class Lesson. Finish with Show What You Know.
Monday night: read your book for 10 minutes. Find one clue to tell Jonathan about.
Tuesday or Wednesday: do the reading lesson Pathways Week 13 Reading: Two Texts, One Harvest. Read two texts and tell how they are the same and different. Aim for 85. If it is locked, type 1111.

slides.title: Word Problem Detective
slides.text: Amy and her friends look for clues. 🔍 Today you look for clues in word problems!

notes.do: Share your screen. Before you start, check that she has about 20 beans (or coins or blocks), a sheet of paper, a pencil and her book next to her.
notes.say: "Amy and her friends are looking for clues. Today you are a detective too. You will look for clues in math stories."
notes.listen: Looks for clues, asks questions, does not guess. Tie it to math: we will not guess the operation.

slides.title: Clues in your book
slides.text: Think about Amy and the Missing Puppy.
prompts: The puppy is missing. What clues help the girls look for it?
If you were Amy, what would you do next?
starters: If I were Amy, I would …

notes.do: Book talk, about 6 minutes. She holds up the page where she stopped.
notes.ask: Ask all three prompts. Push for a real clue from the text: "Show me the sentence."
notes.listen: A clue that comes from the book (where the puppy was seen, who saw it). If she says "I don't know", read one page aloud together and find one clue.

items.q:
8 × 6 = ?
Hint: double the 4s fact.
no: 42 is 7 × 6. Find 4 × 6 first, then double it.
54 is 9 × 6. Find 4 × 6 = 24, then double it.

items.q:
9 × 7 = ?
Hint: 10 sevens, take away one 7.
no: 56 is 8 × 7. You need 9 sevens.
72 is 9 × 8. Use 10 × 7 = 70, then take away 7.

items.q: There are 6 shelves. Each shelf has 7 books. Which number sentence fits?
items.why: Each shelf has 7, so the groups are equal. 6 × 7 = 42.
no: Adding counts only one shelf of books. Every shelf has 7.
There are 6 shelves, not 7.

notes.do: You tap for her. Before each answer, she says the strategy out loud.
notes.ask: "8 × 6: what is 4 × 6 first?" "9 × 7: what is 10 × 7?" "Shelves: is every shelf the same?"
notes.listen: Double the 4s for ×8 (24 → 48). 10 sevens take away one 7 for ×9 (70 − 7 = 63). If she guesses, ask for the strategy before the answer.

slides.title: Don't grab the numbers!
slides.text:
Amy has 4 bags. Each bag has 6 bones. How many bones?
A number grabber says: 4 + 6 = 10. 🤔

steps.text: Let's draw it. 4 bags. 6 bones in each bag.
Count the bones: 6, 12, 18, 24. Not 10!
The numbers were right. The operation was wrong. It is 4 × 6 = 24.

slides.tip: Good detectives read the story first. Then they pick the operation.

notes.do: Show the story and the 4 + 6 = 10 answer first. Do NOT reveal the steps yet. Have her put out 4 piles of 6 beans on her table and hold them up to the camera.
notes.say: "Someone grabbed the 4 and the 6 and added them. Let's see if 10 is right."
notes.ask: "Is 10 bones right? Count your beans. How many?" Then: "Were the numbers wrong, or was the plus sign wrong?"
notes.listen: "24" and "the plus was wrong." Name the habit gently: "That is called number grabbing. Today we stop doing it."

slides.title: The 3 detective questions

steps.text: 1. What is happening? Tell the story in your own words.
2. Are there equal groups? Look for each, every or per.
3. Which operation? ➕ add, ➖ subtract or ✖️ multiply?

slides.tip: Do not grab the numbers first. Ask the questions first!

notes.do: Reveal one question at a time. She repeats each question after you. Then say all three together twice with hand signals: 1 finger, 2 fingers, 3 fingers.
notes.say: "Before we solve, we ask 3 questions. Every story. Every time."
notes.ask: Hide the slide (stop sharing for 10 seconds): "Tell me the 3 questions."
notes.listen: All 3 in order, in her words: What is happening? Are the groups equal? Add, subtract or multiply? Repeat until she says them without looking.

slides.title: Three kinds of stories
slides.text: Most stories are one of these 3 kinds.

steps.text:
➕ Put together. Two different amounts join.
Liz has 6 fish. Marion has 2 fish. How many fish?
Add: 6 + 2 = 8

➖ Take away or compare. Some go away, or you find how many more.
There are 9 kittens. 3 go home. How many are left?
Subtract: 9 − 3 = 6

✖️ Equal groups. Every group has the same number.
There are 4 pens. Each pen has 5 rabbits.
Multiply: 4 × 5 = 20

slides.tip: Equal groups → ✖️. Different amounts join → ➕. Some go away, or how many more → ➖.

notes.do: Reveal each kind. After each one she acts it out with her beans on camera: join two piles (add); take some away (subtract); make equal piles (multiply).
notes.ask: After the take-away story: "What did the beans do?" After equal groups: "Is every pen the same?"
notes.listen: Join = add, go away or compare = subtract, same in every group = multiply. If she says "take away" for the compare idea, accept it and add: "How many more also means subtract."

slides.title: Build the nests
slides.text: There are 5 nests. Each nest has 3 eggs. Make the groups.
slides.why: 5 nests. 3 eggs in each nest. 5 × 3 = 15 eggs.
slides.hint: How many nests? That is the groups. How many eggs in each nest?

notes.do: She builds it with beans first (5 piles of 3), then tells you the numbers and you set the counters on screen.
notes.ask: "What is happening? Are the groups equal? Which operation?" Then: "How many groups? How many in each?"
notes.listen: 5 groups, 3 in each, multiply, 15. If she makes 3 groups of 5, ask: "What are the groups in this story: nests or eggs?"

slides.title: What is happening?
slides.text: Read the story. Say what is happening. Then pick the box.

items.text: Amy's mom has 8 cages. Each cage has 2 rabbits.
items.hint: Find the word each. Is every cage the same?

items.text: Ellie had 15 stickers. She gave 6 to Liz.
items.hint: Did Ellie get stickers or give some away?

items.text: Marion rode her bike 7 miles. Then she rode 4 more miles.
items.hint: Two different amounts join. Nothing goes away.

items.text: Liz has 12 crayons. Amy has 5. How many more does Liz have?
items.hint: How many more asks you to compare.

items.text: There are 6 vans. Every van has 4 seats.
A puppy had 10 treats. It ate 7 of them.
items.hint: Did the treats join or go away?

items.text: The club washed 5 dogs in the morning and 8 dogs after lunch.
items.why: 5 and 8 are different amounts that join. 5 + 8.

slides.done: Join ➕. Take away or compare ➖. Equal groups ✖️.

notes.do: She reads each story card aloud and says what is happening in her own words BEFORE she names the box. You tap the card, then the box she names. The three boxes match the 3 kinds of stories from slide 6.
notes.ask: "What is happening?" then "Equal groups?" then "Which box?"
notes.listen: The crayons card (Liz 12, Amy 5): "how many more" means compare, so subtract. The 5 dogs and 8 dogs card: different amounts join, so add (not multiply). If she names the wrong box, tap it anyway so she sees the hint, then ask the 3 questions again.

slides.title: A detective at work
slides.text: Amy's mom checks 7 dogs. Each dog gets 4 treats. How many treats?

steps.text: 1. What is happening? Every dog gets some treats.
2. Equal groups? Yes! Each dog gets 4.
3. Which operation? 7 groups of 4 → ✖️
Solve. 7 × 4 = 28 treats.
Check. Double, double: 7 → 14 → 28. ✔

slides.tip: Draw it! Make 7 circles. Put 4 dots in each circle.

notes.do: I do. Reveal one step at a time and think out loud. Draw 7 circles with 4 dots each on the Zoom whiteboard (or paper held to the camera).
notes.say: "Watch me be the detective. I ask question 1 … question 2 … question 3. Now I solve. Now I check."
notes.ask: At the end: "Why did I not add 7 + 4?"
notes.listen: "Because each dog gets 4. It is equal groups."

slides.title: Solve it together
slides.text: The vet sees 6 cats in the morning. She sees 9 cats after lunch. How many cats?

steps.text: 1. What is happening? Two groups of cats come in. They join.
2. Equal groups? No. 6 and 9 are different amounts.
3. Which operation? Join different amounts → ➕ add.
Solve. 6 + 9 = 15 cats. Check: 9 + 6 = 15 too. ✔

slides.tip: Not every story is multiply! Different amounts → add.

notes.do: We do. She answers each question out loud BEFORE you reveal the step. She draws the picture on her paper and holds it up.
notes.ask: "What is happening?" "Are 6 and 9 equal groups?" "Which operation?" "What is 6 + 9?"
notes.listen: Add, 15. Watch for 6 × 9 = 54: she saw two numbers and multiplied. Ask: "Is every group the same size?"

items.q: Liz has 8 marbles. She loses 3. How many are left? What would you draw?
no: She did not get more. She lost 3.
There are no equal groups. Marbles went away.

items.q: There are 3 hutches. Each hutch has 6 bunnies. How many bunnies? What would you draw?
choices: A group of 3 bunnies and a group of 6 bunnies
no: That picture shows 3 + 6. But each hutch has 6.
That switches them. How many hutches? 3.

items.q: Marion has 5 hats. Ellie has 7 hats. How many hats in all? What would you draw?
choices: A group of 5 hats and a group of 7 hats
no: There are not 5 groups. Each girl has her own hats.
No hats went away. The story asks how many in all.

notes.do: She reads each story aloud and describes the picture she would draw BEFORE she looks at the choices. You tap.
notes.ask: "Tell me the picture in your head first."
notes.listen: For the hutches: 3 hutches with 6 in each (not 6 with 3 in each). Ask: "How many hutches? That is the number of groups."

slides.title: Watch out for trap words!
slides.text: Some words can trick you. Read the whole story.

steps.text:
"In all" does not always mean add.
There are 5 packs. Each pack has 6 pencils. How many pencils in all?
Equal groups → 5 × 6 = 30

"More" can mean add or subtract.
Liz has 9 pens. She gets 4 more. → add: 9 + 4 = 13
Liz has 9 pens. Amy has 4 pens. How many more does Liz have? → subtract: 9 − 4 = 5

slides.tip: How many more asks you to compare. Compare means subtract.

notes.do: Reveal one step at a time. Show 5 packs of 6 with beans if she needs it.
notes.say: "Some words try to trick us. 'In all' can be add or multiply. 'More' can be add or subtract. So we read the WHOLE story."
notes.ask: "Liz gets 4 more pens: do the pens join or do we compare?" "How many MORE does Liz have: join or compare?"
notes.listen: Gets more → join → add. How many more → compare → subtract.

items.q:
Marion has 11 stickers. Ellie has 6. How many more does Marion have?
Add, subtract or multiply?
items.no: Are the stickers joining, or are we comparing two girls?

items.q: There are 5 boxes. Each box has 9 crayons. How many crayons in all?
items.why: Each box has 9. Equal groups, so multiply: 5 × 9 = 45.
no: In all tricked you. Each box has 9, so it is equal groups.
Nothing goes away. Every box has 9 crayons.

notes.do: Quick check for understanding. She answers out loud; you type or tap what she says.
notes.ask: For the first one: "Is anything joining?" For the second: "Does 'in all' mean add here? Why not?"
notes.listen: "Subtract, because we compare." "Multiply, because each box has 9." If she misses either, go back one slide and reread the trap word step.

slides.title: Detective steps
slides.text: Tap the steps in the right order.
slides.why: That is the detective routine! Read, ask 3 questions, solve, check.
slides.hint: What do you do before anything else?

notes.do: You tap the steps in the order she says them.
notes.ask: "What is the very first thing a detective does?"
notes.listen: Read the whole story first. If she starts with "pick the operation", ask: "How can you pick before you know what is happening?"

slides.title: Tell me a story
slides.text: Make up your own stories. Your teacher will draw them.

notes.do: She makes up each story. You draw exactly what she says on the whiteboard, even if it does not match the number sentence.
notes.ask: After each story: "Does my picture show 6 × 4?"
notes.listen: A multiply story needs equal groups (6 bags with 4 in each). If she tells "6 dogs and 4 cats" for 6 × 4, draw it and ask: "Are those equal groups?"

items.q: The vet has 9 boxes of bandages. Each box has 6 bandages. How many bandages?
no: 15 is 9 + 6. That counts only one box. Every box has 6.
45 is 9 × 5. Each box has 6, not 5.

items.q: Amy has 14 dog treats. Ellie has 8. How many more does Amy have?
no: 22 is 14 + 8. How many more means subtract.
Count up from 8 to 14: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14. That is 6, not 7.

items.q: Marion picks 8 apples. Liz picks 8 apples. Amy picks 8 apples. How many apples?
no: 16 is only 2 girls. Count the girls: 3.
11 is 8 + 3. There are 3 groups of 8.

notes.do: Guided practice. She reads each story aloud, answers the 3 questions out loud, then tells you the answer. You tap.
notes.ask: "What is happening? Equal groups? Which operation?" Then the fact strategy: 9 × 6 = 10 sixes take away one 6.
notes.listen: 54, 6, 24. For the apples, she should see 3 equal groups even with no word "each" (8, 8, 8).

slides.title: What did you learn?
prompts: Say the 3 detective questions from memory.
Which words tell you the groups are equal?

notes.listen: The 3 questions in order; each, every or per; compare, so subtract.
